name: Cryptic crossword No 22,191
preamble: In one way or another, each across solution has a 10 19.

clue.text: Whiskey and biscuits?

definitions.note: plural clue word; the answer names the kind of biscuit

blocks.note: first meaning: an American whiskey distilled mainly from corn
second meaning: a chocolate-filled sandwich biscuit sold in Britain

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the biscuits are a brand-style name: a Bourbon is a British chocolate cream biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: Kentucky corn spirit carries this name, and so does an oblong chocolate cream sandwich cookie popular in Britain.

clue.text: Lowry and 8 almost cultivated a control freak

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the referenced entry loses its final letter
cultivated ground is turned over and worked, so the letters are dug up and rearranged

blocks.note: the painter L. S. Lowry, known by his initials
the answer to 8 across

explanation.surface: An odd pairing of a Salford painter and a medieval royal dynasty somehow grows into a domineering manipulator.
explanation.walkthrough: L. S. Lowry was the Salford painter of matchstick figures; his initials go with the 8-across answer minus its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Svengali is the sinister hypnotist in du Maurier's novel Trilby, whose name now means anyone who manipulates and dominates another person.

clue.text: Vicious Lord 14 captured Frome, briefly

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor, so one piece sits within the other
briefly means cut short, so the name loses its last letter

blocks.note: Lord Lieutenant, the 14-across word in the singular, abbreviated by its initials
Ethan Frome, title hero of Edith Wharton's novel; his first name

explanation.surface: A cruel county grandee has seized the Somerset town of Frome in a quick raid.
explanation.walkthrough: Frome looks like the Somerset town, but it is Ethan Frome of Wharton's novel, whose first name is clipped. A Lord Lieutenant is the Crown's representative in a British county.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lethal can kill, and a vicious blow or attack is savage enough to be deadly.

clue.text: Flashes retreating Scots' own soldiers at half nine

indicators.note: troops retreating go back the way they came, so the whole string runs backwards up the column
half of a word keeps only part of it, so the second pair of letters is dropped

blocks.note: ain is the Scots word for own
GIs are American soldiers
the first half of the word nine

explanation.surface: Scottish troops in retreat with their own soldiers flash something at half past eight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flashes' looks like a verb, but it is a noun: the badges sewn on a uniform sleeve. The reversal covers all three pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: Military flashes are the cloth badges on uniform showing unit or rank, which are insignia.

clue.text: Girl's end upset Lysander's admirer

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, which in a down entry reads a word bottom to top

blocks.note: the possessive belonging to a girl
an end is a goal or aim

explanation.surface: A girl's purpose has been thwarted, which unsettles a young man named Lysander who admires her.
explanation.walkthrough: Lysander and Hermia are the eloping lovers in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's comedy the young woman Hermia loves Lysander and flees Athens with him against her father's wishes.

clue.text: Cockney motto expressing dejection

indicators.note: a Cockney accent turns the long a vowel into a long i, so the word is heard as a London speaker says it

blocks.note: a motto is a saying, and in Cockney speech saying comes out with an eye sound

explanation.surface: A gloomy East Ender's watchword, voiced as a weary expression of low spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class London accent, in which day sounds like die; so a saying is heard as a sighing.
explanation.definitionFit: A sigh is a long audible breath let out in sadness, so sighing shows dejection.

clue.text: Strips to relieve stuffiness in galleries

definitions.note: plural: the Paris art gallery made plural

blocks.note: first meaning: angled slats in a window or vent that let air through
second meaning: more than one of the great Paris art museum

explanation.surface: Ventilation slats are fitted to freshen the air in stuffy art galleries.
explanation.walkthrough: The French link is the Louvre in Paris, the world's largest art museum; the plural lets it match the slats.
explanation.definitionFit: Ventilation slats set at an angle across an opening are louvres, and the Louvre is the famous Paris museum.

clue.text: Plantagenet raised greens, perhaps, eaten by Miss Bawden

indicators.note: food eaten by someone ends up inside them, so one piece goes within the name
raised means lifted up and turned, so the combined letters are read from the end back

blocks.note: greens are an example of vegetables, short form veg
Nina Bawden, the English novelist

explanation.surface: A medieval king grows vegetables which the children's author Nina Bawden then eats.
explanation.walkthrough: Nina Bawden wrote Carrie's War. The reversal covers her name with the vegetables already inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plantagenet kings descended from the Counts of Anjou, so the dynasty is also called Angevin, a word of French origin.

clue.text: They possess firm making quality starch and canvas

blocks.note: first meaning: things with the property of making something rigid
second meaning: two materials used to make collars and lapels rigid

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'firm making' as making firm; starch and canvas are the classic examples, used in shirt collars and tailoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Tailors and launderers use substances such as starch and interfacing canvas to add rigidity, and these are called stiffenings.

clue.text: Mon Oncle, the film

blocks.note: surface reading: the Jacques Tati comedy Mon Oncle
setter's reading: my uncle in the language of Paris, that is, a relative from across the Channel, which titles a 1971 crime thriller

explanation.walkthrough: Mon Oncle means my uncle, a relation who is French; and the answer is also the 1971 Gene Hackman drugs thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncle is a family connection, and one called mon oncle is French; the phrase is also a famous film title.

clue.text: Mother! Pi was concocted to describe an arc

definitions.note: the word that names the famous Paris arch

indicators.note: something concocted is made up by mixing ingredients, so these letters are blended into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mother exclaims as a maths constant is cooked up to measure a curve.
explanation.walkthrough: The arc is the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, so the word describes it; 'arc' looks like geometry next to pi.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's great Paris arch is the Arc de Triomphe, so the French word for triumph completes and describes that arc.

clue.text: Nana's dad is dribbling at Stamford Bridge

definitions.note: names the player rather than the action

blocks.note: first meaning: the French novelist who created the novel Nana
second meaning: the Italian footballer Gianfranco, who played for Chelsea

explanation.surface: A grandmother's father is seen dribbling at a London football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Nana looks like a granny, but it is Emile Zola's novel. Stamford Bridge is the home ground of Chelsea Football Club in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Emile Zola wrote Nana, making him its literary father; Gianfranco Zola dribbled brilliantly for Chelsea in the late 1990s.

clue.text: A type-face inspired by cultured Elian fabulist

indicators.note: something inspired is breathed in, so one group of letters is drawn into the other
cultured suggests grown and cultivated, so the name's letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
a typeface is a font
taken as written

explanation.surface: A refined person called Elian is inspired by a particular typeface when writing fables.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of Elian are rearranged and A FONT goes in after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean de La Fontaine was the seventeenth-century French poet famous for his Fables, so he is the classic fabulist.

clue.text: It's novel, when woman backs this after 10

blocks.clueFragment: It's novel, when woman backs this after 10
blocks.note: surface reading: an odd remark about a woman supporting something
setter's reading: put the answer after the 10-across word and follow it with woman, and you have the title of John Fowles's 1969 novel

explanation.walkthrough: The novel is John Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman; 'backs' means comes at the back of, not supports.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowles's book title is The French Lieutenant's Woman, so the missing middle word, with its possessive s, is this one.

clue.text: No longer going round and round, cold drunk sits under a 10

definitions.text: No longer going round and round

indicators.note: in a down entry, sitting under something means coming after it in the column

blocks.note: a in French, the 10-across language
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps
oiled is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Someone stops spinning after a drunk who feels the cold sits down beneath a Frenchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A rope or spring that has been unwound is uncoiled, so it no longer runs in circles.

clue.text: Thanks to Barrie or Synge, who wrote on a prince building a mausoleum

indicators.note: in a down entry, on means placed above, so the earlier pieces sit on top of the later ones

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thanks
both playwrights, J. M. Barrie and J. M. Synge, shared these initials
taken as written
Prince Hal, the young Henry V in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A writer of Peter Pan or of Irish plays is thanked for a book on a prince who erected a tomb.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta is British for thanks. Barrie and Synge are both writers with the initials J. M.
explanation.definitionFit: Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra as a tomb for his wife, making it the most famous mausoleum in the world.

clue.text: Taking off, at first, is not so easy for a squirrel

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter only of the word just before it
taking means taking in, so one letter is received within the longer word

blocks.note: less easy, the comparative of hard
the opening letter of off

explanation.surface: Getting airborne is tougher than it looks for a squirrel leaping from a branch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a flying squirrel taking off; instead the opening letter of off goes into the comparative.
explanation.definitionFit: Squirrels bury nuts for winter, and figuratively a squirrel is a person who stockpiles things, a hoarder.

clue.text: Smith's job, they say, is telling folk to push off

indicators.note: they say points to what people say out loud, so the sound of the phrase matters rather than its spelling

blocks.note: driving people away with shoo

explanation.surface: A blacksmith's job, apparently, involves sending customers on their way.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith looks like a surname, but it means a blacksmith, who fits horseshoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A blacksmith or farrier nails iron shoes on horses' hooves, and that work is called shoeing.

clue.text: See 10
Space travellers heartlessly ruined organ stop

indicators.note: heartlessly means with the heart taken out, so only the two end letters stay

blocks.note: the American space agency
the first and last letters of ruined

explanation.surface: Astronauts cruelly wreck a church organ's stop.
explanation.definitionFit: A nasard is a flute-like mutation stop on a pipe organ sounding a twelfth above the note played.

clue.text: Take away top and bottom drawers for £1?

indicators.note: removing the top and bottom of a down word drops its first and last letters

blocks.note: drawers is an old word for underpants

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a pair of underwear can be removed from top to bottom for a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: Knickers are British women's underpants. 'Take away' sounds like stealing, but it strips the ends of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicker is British slang for a pound sterling, plural also nicker, much like quid.

clue.text: He, one of the Loos (WW1) top brass, sir, stands before 10

definitions.note: the person is the WW1 commander, Sir John French

blocks.note: first meaning: a toilet, in American slang
second meaning: the first name of the British commander at the Battle of Loos, whose surname is the 10-across word

explanation.walkthrough: Loos is a 1915 battle in France where Sir John French commanded the British; read as loos, it is lavatories.
explanation.definitionFit: A john is slang for a lavatory, and Field Marshal Sir John French led the British Expeditionary Force in 1914 and 1915.

clue.text: Putting on the sauce

blocks.note: first meaning: getting clothes on
second meaning: an oil and vinegar mixture poured on salad

explanation.surface: Someone is pouring sauce on their food, or perhaps hitting the bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting on the sauce' sounds like drinking (on the sauce), but the meanings are separate. The French link is French dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Dressing is the act of clothing oneself and also a liquid seasoning poured over salad.

clue.text: Designer launches out, leaving us behind

indicators.note: leaving something behind means going without it, so those letters drop out
out suggests disorder, letters knocked out of place and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; these are removed

explanation.surface: A fashion designer launches a new collection and leaves the rest of us behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Coco Chanel was the French couturier who founded the Paris fashion house bearing her name.

clue.text: Blunder into kind of glass of water

indicators.note: into means going inside something, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: to blunder is to make a mistake
a pier glass is a tall mirror hung between windows

explanation.surface: Someone clumsily knocks into a glass of water.
explanation.walkthrough: A pier glass is a tall wall mirror; 'glass of water' tempts a solver to read the whole phrase as a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Perrier is a French brand of sparkling mineral water from a spring in the south of France.

clue.text: Painter cut husband at the home of Frank?

indicators.note: cut means trimmed, so a letter is removed from the French phrase

blocks.note: the French word for at the home of
H is the abbreviation for husband; this is removed
Anne Frank, the young Amsterdam diarist

explanation.surface: An artist drops her husband while staying at the house of a man called Frank.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank looks like a man's first name, but it is the surname of the diarist Anne Frank.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Cezanne was the French Post-Impressionist painter of Mont Sainte-Victoire and still lifes of apples.
